nodes.title: TAXONOMY
nodes.body:
Scientific Name: Anchoa mitchilli (Cuvier and Vanciennes 1848, listed in 1533)
Subspecific Names: There are two subspecies of the bay anchovy, Anchoa mitchilli mitchilli and Anchoa mitchilli diaphana (309).  A. mitchilli mitchilli generally are more slender than A. mitchilli diaphana, are less strongly compressed, have more vertebrae, have the dorsal fin farther back, and have shorter pectoral fins (309).  The depth of A. mitchilli diaphana increases in proportion to its standard length (SL) from the northern range southward (309).

Synonyms: The following synonyms are listed in Olsen (1533):
	Engraulis mitchilli, Cuvier and Vanciennes 1848
	Stolephorous mitchilli, Jordan and Gilbert 1882
	Anchovia mitchilli, Fowler 1905
	Anchoviella mitchilli, Jordan and Seale 1926
Common Name: Bay anchovy
Other Common Names: anchovy (312 834); glass minnow (664); southern bay anchovy (378 581); common anchovy, mitchill`s anchovy, whitebait, little anchovy (794), anchois bai (French), and anchoa de caleta (Spanish) (791).

nodes.title: Classification

	Class:	            Steichthyes
	Order:	            Lupeiformes
	Family:	Engraulidae

Taxonomic Characteristics (by life stages):
Young of Year:

nodes.title: Juvenile
nodes.body:
Adult: Adult bay anchovy is described as having: origin of anal fin under or slightly posterior to the dorsal fin origin, distinguishing them from other anchovies; short rounded protuberant snout (no more than 1/4 its length) projecting beyond the tip of the mandible; a large mouth; a cheek short and broad with a length approximately that of the eye;  pointed enlarged maxillary, near margin of opercule; the dorsal fin low with a nearly straight margin; the anal fin slightly posterior or under fifth or sixth dorsal ray; a small pelvic fin, not measuring halfway to origin of anal fin; variable pectoral fins, not reaching base of pelvic fin by distance equal to or greater than diameter of the eye; greenish with bluish reflections above the silvery narrow lateral band lined with scales; iridescent green-and-gold patch on the skull shields the brain dorsally; translucent abdominal walls; seldom exceeding a total length of 100 mm (4 in); and averaging 75 mm (159 311 327 366).

Similar Species:  Anchoa hepsetus (striped anchovy) (1504),  Anchoa parva, A. cubana, A. lamprotaenia, A. cayorum, A. lyolepis, A. filifera, Anchoviella and Engrualis eurystole (791).

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body:
Overall: The bay anchovy occurs from Maine to Mexico, and is the most abundant species of fish within estuaries along the U.S. Atlantic coast (159 327 309 311 342 788 791 1568).

 It is a nearshore, coastal, estuarine species (1568).  They maintain a relatively fixed location, never really straying more than a few miles from their area of birth their entire lives (309 339 1552 1568).  It occurs from Casco Bay, Maine to Vera Cruz, Rio Panuco, Tampico, Mexico (159 327 309 311 342 788 791 835).  It is taken only rarely in Yucatan, Gulf of Maine, and Florida Keys and never in the West Indies (159 327 309 791).  The bay anchovy is the most abundant species of fish within estuaries along the U.S. Atlantic coast (1568).  In an intertidal creek in South Carolina, the bay anchovy accounted for 96.3% of the total number of individuals sampled (1549).

A. mitchilli diaphana ranges from the Yucatan to South Carolina and A. mitchilli mitchilli extends from North Carolina to Maine, although the southern limit for the later subspecies is indefinite (309 891).  It has also been shown by morphometric methods that virtually every section of the coast within its range, the bay anchovy has a distinctive population (309 311).

nodes.title: By State
nodes.body:
Florida:  Bay anchovies are abundant in coastal and estuarine waters throughout Florida (265 378 664 848).  It is the most abundant fish species in Everglades National Park`s brackish waters (702 1373).  The bay anchovy occurs primarily in open bays and in the Florida Keys (327 664).

By Stock:  A. mitchilli diaphana is found in western Floridian waters while a mixture of both A. mitchilli diaphana and A. mitchilli mitchilli is found in eastern Floridian waters and (309).

nodes.title: By Estuary
nodes.body:
Indian River lagoon:  The bay anchovy comprised 75% of the fish collected over seagrasses (1006) and was the most abundant fish collected overall (997 1006).
Tampa Bay:  Bay anchovy are distributed widely throughout Tampa Bay in all seasons of the year and in both deep and shallow water habitats.  Drop nets in seagrass beds collected few bay anchovies (1520).  Larval densities are greatest from March through August (1339).
Florida Bay: The bay anchovy is considered abundant in Florida Bay`s coastal and estuarine waters (835 1425).  It is the most abundant water column forage species reported for collections made in northeast Florida Bay (1422).  Sogard et al. (1243) found that striped and bay anchovies made up more that 48% of all fish they collected in western and southwestern Florida Bay.  However, Thayer and Chester (1431) reported that bay anchovies constituted only 15% of their total catch in channels and basins in central and western Florida Bay.  Adults and juveniles are considered “highly abundant” in Florida Bay`s mixing and seawater zones (1522).  Adult and juveniles are listed as “abundant” in Tidal Fresh zone (1522).
Sarasota Bay:  Maximum densities of bay anchovy occur in the spring, with a secondary peak in the late summer/early autumn (1351).  Bay anchovy eggs are present year round, except January (1351).  Larvae are found to be more abundant in open water bay area`s than in the Gulf passes (1351).
Spatial Strategy: Bay anchovies primarily occupy the upper 15 m of the water column (1576).  Movement into deeper waters occurs during winter, while returning inshore during summer (116 309 311 366 1350).  Environmental fluctuations (i.e. anoxia during the summer, cold stress during the winter) influence the variability of depth distribution (1576).  Throughout all life stages, the bay anchovy is pelagic (1568).
Egg:  Eggs are free floating throughout the water column, but primarily found near the surface (1530).
Larva:  Spawning occurs in bays, estuaries, tidal passes, and offshore, with significant transport of larvae inshore (322 39 614 366 754 1521 1559).  Larvae are reported to migrate into lower salinity nursery areas while developing toward the juvenile stage (197 322 696 1337 1350 1521).  Peak larval movement into a Texas tidal pass occurred in June (9).
Young-of-Year:  Not applicable.
Juvenile:  Juveniles have been found to congregate in brackish waters very close to the salt/fresh water interface as they develop toward adulthood (1007). Juveniles then move to deeper, more saline areas in early fall (197 322 696 1337 1350 1521)
Adult:  Bay anchovies are primarily a shallow estuarine and inshore coastal water species (366 19 696 664 378 255 644 646 754).  Studies show the bay anchovy is able to exploit a wide variety of habitats such as: bays and bayous, off sandy beaches, grassy areas along beaches, muddy coves,  mouths of rivers, and both shallow and deeper waters offshore (366 582 644 366), but prefers bays and estuaries to shallow waters of the Gulf of Mexico (116 255 378 664). In Galveston Bay, bay anchovies were found to prefer sand and silt bottoms to oyster reefs (226).  Population density appears to be influenced by the mass of zooplankton present (582 1562) which probably accounts for their preference of bays and, when found in the Gulf, bay water masses (322). They are particularly common in primary and secondary bays, around shallow bay margins, islands, spoil banks, and sheltered coves, but scarce in tertiary bays (378 651 694 754).  Reports show that bay anchovies occur from fresh to hypersaline waters (550 651 366).  In an intertidal creek of South Carolina, increased numbers of adults occurred when the area flooded during daylight hours, but reduced numbers when flooding occurred at night (1549).

In a Louisiana estuary, a species turnover in spring occurred as gulf menhaden, the dominant water column species from winter leading to spring, was replaced by bay anchovy (1540).  These changes were associated with changes in temperature, DO, possible ecological interactions between species, and particularly salinity (1540).

In a South Carolina estuary, immigration of adults in the spring resulted in a redistribution of planktivore species, as Atlantic silversides shifted to surface waters and bay anchovies dominated the lower half of the water column (1539).  Spring to summer in this region showed bay anchovies widely distributed in the surface and bottom water columns until striped anchovies and rough silversides dominated the surface from mid-summer through fall (1539).

Mobility/Migration:  Studies have found that activity is primarily nocturnal (159 786 1563), associated with predator avoidance (1528).  Dixon et al. (1579) found that CPUE of bay anchovy was significantly higher during night cruises in their study in Virginia.  Other observations show that bay anchovies are more abundant during daylight hours, thus more susceptible to predatory capture (1560 1549).

Bay anchovies are considered sedentary, as individuals do not stray far from their place of birth (309).  Migrations occur seasonally, typically between onshore and offshore habitats (116 309 311 366 1350).  In winter, bay anchovies do not migrate to lower, warmer latitudes, but move from shallow water to deeper bay waters (1337).  A reverse effect occurs in the spring (1560 1337).

Egg:  Eggs are pelagic and found throughout the water column, but most abundant on the surface (322 327 342 392 582 754 1530).
Larva: Small larvae are initially planktonic (1530) as older larvae are primarily nektonic (392 582 322 163 165 366 1530).  Larvae generally occupy the upper portion of the water column (311 366 1544).  Mean larval length and 5.5 mm larvae abundance increased in an offshore to inshore direction in Chesapeake Bay (1559).
Young-of-Year:  Since the bay anchovy reaches the adult stage within the first year, Young-of-Year encompasses all life stages.  This life stage is not applicable.
Juvenile:  Juveniles are primarily nektonic and largely found in deeper estuarine waters, compared to larvae (163 165 311 322 366 392 582 1544).
Adult:  Adults are primarily nektonic (392 582 322 163 165 366).  They are mostly found in inshore waters, but also occur in offshore waters for spawning (311 366 1559).

Symbiotic: No symbiotic behavior known.

Schooling: Bay anchovies school in large numbers during the day (339 1552).  Schooling is mainly dependent on vision, as bay anchovies have no posterior lateral lines which some species rely on for monitoring speed and direction of other fish in the school (1552).  Observations show this species to form small schools while feeding at night as well (19 159 309 327 754).

nodes.title: BENTHIC HABITAT
nodes.body:
Substrate:  Although found in a variety of habitats, substrate types apparently are of little significance in the distribution of bay anchovies (1349 1521 1568).  This is further supported by Castro and Cowan (1556) as no difference was found between eelgrass and unvegetated areas pertaining to egg or larval density, larval growth rates, and egg and yolk sac larvae mortalities.  Ley (1422), however, noted that anchovies exhibited a preference for sites with sparse growths of submerged vegetation.

Bay anchovies have occurred over bottoms of: clay, hard sand, silty clay, clayey silt, silt and sand, sandy mud, muddy sand, and seagrass beds (140 193 185 224 311 325 378 581 582 694 709 1348).

Submerged Vegetation: Vegetation is of little significance in the distribution of bay anchovies, even though reduced anchovy numbers are associated with seagrass beds (1349 1521 1534 1568).  Predation in this area is responsible for lesser bay anchovy abundance (1560 1549).  Anchovies collected in vegetated areas have lower body weights than those collected from unvegetated areas, suggesting that the species is less successful at foraging in dense vegetation (1534).

Depth Distribution (by life stage):
Egg:  Few eggs are found below the pynocline in Chesapeake Bay, where oxygen levels are often too low for survival or normal development (1559).  Marley (1565) observed in Mobile Bay, AL that eggs were confined to bottom waters when river discharge was high, but equally divided between bottom and surface waters when river discharge was low.
Larva:  Larvae are usually found in depths of less than 3 m (1568).  Marked vertical changes in abundance of feeding stage larvae are defined by behavioral responses to O2 gradients (1525).  Few larvae are observed below the pynocline in Chesapeake Bay, where oxygen levels are often too low for survival or normal development (1559).
Young-of-Year:  Not applicable.
Juvenile:  Juveniles are usually found in depths of less than 3 m (1568).
Adult: Adults are water column species that use surface waters when bottom O2 concentrations are low (1525).  Usually found in shallow depths, the bay anchovy has been collected in waters depths from 0.5-36 m, appearing to prefer 2-3 m (39 185 193 224 325 550 582 588 694 791 1568).  Changes in seasonal and diurnal depth distribution are not clearly understood (1568).

nodes.title: Temperature
nodes.body:
Egg: Spawning and egg development have been recorded from 13-32 degrees C (174 342 392 1568). Preferred water temperatures are generally in the upper twenties (degrees C) (754 1339 1568).  In Tampa Bay, spawning begins when water temperatures reach 20 degrees C (1339).  However, specific temperature above this mark is not a significant factor for reproduction, as it did not account for variations in egg abundances (1566).
Larva:  Temperatures preferred by larvae are from 15-30 C (1568).  Estimated larval densities in Tampa Bay were strongly correlated with water temperature (1504), however there is no significant correlation between larva growth rate and temperature (1335).
Young-of-Year:  Not applicable.
Juvenile:  Juveniles are considered eurythermal (1544), but are more abundant in the warmer estuarine waters.
Adult:	Adults are also considered eurythermal, occurring in water temperatures ranging from 2-40 C (255 582 378 651 588 664 325 224 550 694 193 751 366 372 561 709 121 887 1373).  The preferred water temperature is between 8.1-32.2 C, usually >11 C (754).  The bay anchovy was not killed in previous Florida freezes (236).  The bay anchovy was found to be one of the three species that dominated water temperatures >23 C in Louisiana (1523).  A possible upper lethal limit of 40 C has been suggested (121).  Adults (mean length of 35mm) were tested and could not survive a temperature of 36 C for 3h (121).

nodes.title: Salinity
nodes.body:
Egg: Spawning and development have occurred from 9-30.9 ppt, and as high as 37 ppt (174 322 342 1340 1350).  Eggs of greatest abundance are found in a salinity range of 13-15 ppt in  Chesapeake Bay (1007).
Larva:  Dovel (1007) noticed 72% of larvae collected in his study in the Chesapeake Bay were found in waters of 3-7 ppt.  In Matagorda Bay, Texas, larvae were found in salinities as low as 0.5-1+ ppt (754).  Larvae tend to move into less saline waters near the freshwater interface, moving back to saltier waters as they mature (255 366 322).
Young-of-Year:  Not applicable.
Juvenile:  Juveniles are more dense in low salinity areas, as a 1-32 ppt range has been seen for juveniles in Matagorda Bay, Texas (754).  Cornelius (140) found a salinity abundance range of 11-20 ppt and 31-40 ppt for juveniles in Alazan Bay, TX.
Adult: Adults are considered euryhaline, collected from waters ranging from 0.0-80 ppt in habitats as diverse as tidal freshwater tributaries and continental shelf waters (255 651 588 197 224 550 694 193 751 366 372 561 664 709 140 1564).  Salinities for Florida collections include: 0.5 ppt in the St. Lucie River, Fl (264 664); from freshwater in the Peace River (789) and Indian River Lagoon, FL (848); 6.2-37.6 ppt at Cedar Key (378); 5.0-36.0 ppt in Tampa Bay (664 853); 0-35.0 ppt in Charlotte Harbor (789); 2.0-38.8 ppt at Jupiter Inlet (887); 0-45.2 ppt in Everglades National Park; and 0.14-28.4 ppt in the Caloosahatchee River with most taken at <1.0 ppt (265).


Recorded preferences in other areas include:  9-30 ppt in Chesapeake Bay; 1-32 ppt in Matagorda Bay, Texas (754); 5 ppt in Copano and Aransas Bays, TX (255); 11-30 ppt in Alazan Bay, TX; <50 ppt in the upper Laguna Madre, Tx (651); 20-29.9 ppt in Mobile and Baldwin counties, AL (694); 0.0-14.9 ppt in Lake Pontchartrain, La. (709); and 2-4.9 ppt along the Mississippi coastline (116).  What this means is that salinity appears to have no relationship to distribution (116 140 255 322 378 391 581 603 664 754 789 1337 1343). Spawning peaks between 13 and 15 ppt (1337).

Dissolved Oxygen:  In Louisiana the bay anchovy was collected in waters with a dissolved oxygen (DO) range of 1.5-11.9 ppm (1519).  DO levels below 3 mg/L probably limit the viability and productivity of the bay anchovy as found in the Chesapeake Bay (1521 1568).  The intrusion of severely hypoxic bottom water does not elicit escape responses of adults and juveniles until oxygen concentrations drop below 0.75 mg l (to the -1), a level strongly avoided by larvae (1525), as levels <1 mg l (to the -1) are lethal for larvae within 24h at 25-27 C (1525).  Posthatch larvae, less than two weeks of age, have threshold tolerances between 1 and 2 mg l (to the -1) during a 24h period (1525).

Turbidity:  Bay anchovy have been collected in water with turbidities of 0.5 m to 0.7 m secchi depth (582 794) It is suggested they are attracted to areas of high turbidity (1343 1568).  Sherk et al. (1573), however, found the bay anchovy to be sensitive to suspended solids.

pH:  No information available

Light/Photoperiod:  Studies have found that activity is primarily nocturnal (159 786), while other observations show that bay anchovy are more active during daylight hours, increasing their vulnerability for predation (1560 1549).  However, the dynamics of light intensity, feeding, and predator avoidance are significantly involved in activity (1549).

nodes.title: Ammonia
nodes.body:
Current/Tides:  During flood tides, larval bay anchovy may move to the middle of tidal passes to maximize transport into estuarine areas (1523).  There is evidence, based on the size of sampled larvae in the Patuxent River, MD, of hydrodynamic transport from downriver spawning areas to upriver nursery grounds (1530).

In laboratory and natural studies, bay anchovy schools break up at night and individuals are transported by currents (1552).  Fish marked with red dye and released in a creek at flood tide were recaptured 5.1 km upstream 4 h after release at night, while a daylight study showed a recapture distance of 200 m, 3 h after release (1578).  Luo (1552) adds that transportation and current speeds indicate that bay anchovies continued to swim in the darkness, but at slower speeds and in random directions.

nodes.title: Trophic Mode
nodes.body:
Eating:  Bay anchovies are primary consumers, feeding predominantly on zooplankton in nocturnal currents (39 159 582), although there is evidence of a relationship between light intensity, feeding, and predator avoidance (1549).  In South Carolina, Johnson et al. (1563) observed bay anchovies feeding through the night, responding to available crustacean larvae from nocturnal hatching, suggesting that feeding selectivity is probably dependent on more than vision alone.

Zooplankton size selection is based on differential encounter rates (1572).  In their study in the Biloxi Bay area (Mississippi), Bin-Din and Gunter (1567) observed the bay anchovy to feed mainly during the early morning with a second minor peak prior to midnight.  Due to predation, the bay anchovy is sometimes unable to exploit the seasonal peak of zooplankton in the Apalachicola Bay (644).  Diel vertical migrations of copepods have been known to influence variable abundances of bay anchovy (1560).

The spawning potential is related to reserved energy, which is, in turn, related to feeding (1561).  In the Chesapeake Bay, consumption is highest in August due to larval and early juvenile growth (1543).

Anchovy larvae have low feeding and growth efficiencies, accounting for its requirement to be located in high densities of prey to compensate for this deficiency (1548).  Zooplankton fluctuations will strongly influence survival and recruitment (1548).

nodes.title: Food Items
nodes.body:
Egg:  Not applicable.
Larva:  Bay anchovy larvae studied 2-8 days after hatching showed that larvae consume approximately twice their body weight in food daily upon initial feeding (1569).  Young individuals are plankton strainers consuming microzooplankton such as copepod nauplii and rotifers until a body length of approximately 7 mm is reached at which time they concentrate on copepodites and copepods (163 174).  Based on laboratory experiments, Houde (1553) found larvae survival rates exceeded 40% when food concentration was 1000 l (to the -1) or higher and Cowan and Houde (1558) observed that highest growth occurred when prey exceeded 1000 l (to the -1) and few larvae survived at prey levels as low as 50 l (to the -1), suggesting that ~100 prey per l (to the -1) is a critical food level.

It is crucial for larvae to find food and develop feeding skills 8h after yolk exhaustion (36h after hatching), as it is this period where the transition from endogenous to exogenous (depletion of yolk-sac) feeding occurs (1548).  However, Houde (342) found that the critical period for first feeding was 2.5 days after hatching.
Young-of-Year:  Not applicable.
Juvenile:  Juveniles are almost exclusively planktivorous, with distinct selection for mulluscan veliger larvae in seagrass beds near Crystal River, FL (98).  Carr and Adams (98) found that gut contents of juveniles 23 mm long revealed approximately equal amounts of copepods and veligers, suggesting a preference in copepods during the latter juvenile stages.  Odum (515) supports this transition, as copepods and copepod larvae are the primary food of anchovies <25 mm long in South Florida estuaries.  Some detritus is also consumed, but phytoplankton is not, suggesting that food straining occurs near the bottom (163).
Adult:  As anchovies grow in size, their diet becomes increasingly selective, shifting from copepods to small shrimp, larval and juvenile fish, macrozooplankton (especially mysids), insect larvae, crab zoeae (especially Uca spp.), clams, cladocerans, schizopods, gastropods, isopods, malacostracans, amphipods, ostracods, small mollusks, and supplemented with detritus from occasional bottom feeding (19 39 98 174 163 165 309 515 581 582 644 759 1337 644 1539 1568).  Gut analysis of individuals 30-49 mm long showed the following diet proportions: 9% microinvertebrates; 58% zooplankton, and 33% organic detritus (165).  Benthic animals and sand are most frequently encountered during the winter suggesting more intensive bottom feeding at this time (163).

In the Apalachicola Bay, Florida, copepods were the dominant prey throughout the year but were markedly less abundant prey during October, December, and February as other crustaceans and insect larvae became more abundant (644).  Areas near the mouth of the Apalachicola River showed mysids, insect larva, and cladocerans as major food items (644).  In the Biloxi Bay, major food items are crustaceans, but calenoid copepods are the most numerically prominent food item (1567).  Also in this area, small plakton are filtered with larger organisms picked individually (1567).  Bay anchovies also show cannabalistic behavior, coinciding with low abundance of other food items (1567).

Most prey items in a South Carolina estuary measured 0.4-3.25 mm in length (1563).  In this area, larger prey dominated the diet around high tide, particularly at night, and small items dominated during the daytime low tide, when larger items were absent (1563).  The crab megalopae were by far the most important species and were favored, even when densities were fewer than comparably sized prey (1563).

nodes.title: Mode
nodes.body:
Domain:  Adult bay anchovies are adept at placing eggs in locations where salinities are constant, zooplankton biomass is high (1504), and the ctenophore Mnemiopsis leidyi is least abundant (1564).  In Tampa Bay, >98% of collected larvae were found with prey densities higher than the suggested threshold prey level for starvation, 100 l (to the -1) (1566).  Kelly and Dragovich (1536) found in their study of Tampa Bay that the highest variety of zooplankton taxa occurs when temperature and salinity are considered high, 28.0-32.0 C and 33.5-36.0 ppt respectively (1536).  Spawning in low-salinity surface waters of well-stratified water columns may protect eggs from ctenophore predation, as co-occurrence increases when water columns mix (1545).

Fertilization:  Fertilization is external, through broadcasting of milt and roe (considered broadcast spawners, batch spawners, serial spawners) (1544 1568).

nodes.title: Spawning Strategy
nodes.body:
Reproductive Periodicity:  Zastrow et al. (1526) found the bay anchovy to spawn 50 to 60 times over several months.  Iteroparity is viewed as a relation of environmental parameters relevant to larval survival -- a seasonal fine tuning of reproductive effort and offspring survival (1566).  Eggs usually are released in the early evening, 1800-2100 h, during warm water (>19 degrees C) periods (185 366 392 322 754 1526).  Luo and Musick (1551) found that spawning in the Chesapeake Bay is temporally synchronized and lasted for ~1.5 h each night.  Spawning time gradually becomes later each month and frequency slows in June (every 4 d) while other months were constant (mean frequency of every 1.3-1.9 d) (1551).  Annual estimated mean spawnings per female in the Chesapeake Bay are 54, with total egg production for average size females is 45,110 (1551).  This is equivalent to 346% of body biomass energy (1551).  Capable of spawning everyday during peak spawning season (1526), dependent on the abundance of food for the energy to do so (1561).  As fish of heavier weight tend to have bigger gonads capable of producing more eggs, a positive correlation between gonad weight and total body weight in female bay anchovies (1561).

Anchovy eggs are abundant from March-October in Apalachicola Bay, FL, (1340). In Tampa Bay, spawning occurs from March through October with peak egg densities occurring from April through July (1019 1339).  Spawning occurs from March through October in Sarasota Bay, Fl with maximum egg densities occurring during the spring (1351).  Some year round spawning is also reported (185 325 550 694 751 754 1019 1339 1340 1351) possibly due to short, usually mild winters which involve warming trends, during which shallow water temperatures approach and exceed 20 degrees C (185 322 1339).

Typical spawning seasons in other parts of the country are: February through August in the Gulf of Mexico near Port Aransas, TX (9 255 322); February to October in Galveston Bay, Texas (39); March through October in Louisiana (188 751 614); February through October, with a July peak, along the Mississippi coastline (116 197); and May until mid-September in Chesapeake Bay (1551).


Spawning Strategy:  Luo (1552) observed that adults drift with the current in the dark, suggesting this behavior allows spawning and eggs to remain with plankton patches located in the daylight.  Spawning strategy is suggested to follow a direct response to increasing temperature, photoperiod (1526 1556), and decreasing salinity (185).  But it is argued that zooplankton rich waters is the main factor for reproduction (1566 1577), based on variations in metabolic rate and adult ration.

Duration of peak spawning season is highly correlated with abundance of food, as adults spawn during the season of maximum food availability to enhance larval survival (1556).  Planktonic larvae are consistently associated with copepod nauplii (1566).  Spawning occurs in waters less than 20 m deep in bays and estuaries, tidal passes, and in the Gulf of Mexico, where it is limited to the shallow inshore areas in bay water masses (322 39 614 366 754 1521).  Vegetated areas are not a preferred spawning zone, as larval mortality from predation increases over these areas (1556).  In the Chesapeake Bay, MacGregor and Houde (1559) found that most spawning occurred offshore, with significant transport of larvae inshore.  Mortality rates are higher offshore and higher for small length class larvae, indicating recruitment of anchovy is most dependent on processes in the offshore region (1559).  Macgregor and Houde (1559) further support this theory by observing an increase in mean larval length and relative abundance in large larvae in an offshore to inshore direction, caused by advection.
Parental Care: Not applicable
Salinities:  In the Apalachicola Bay, spawning occurs at salinities above 9-10 ppt (1340 1350) with greatest activity at salinities near 20 ppt (1340).  In Tampa Bay, spawning usually does not occur until the water temperatures reach 20 degrees C (1339).  Some spawning has been observed in higher salinity portions of estuaries with ranges of 30-37 ppt, with <45 ppt being reported (39 185 366).  In the Patuxent River, MD, spawning has occurred in waters as low as 1 ppt, usually not below 6 ppt, and a maximum spawning in waters with salinity ranging between 13-15 ppt (1530).
Seasonal Energetics: Energy storage is dynamic and changes seasonally (1543).  Body weight of both males and females increases before spawning, decreases during initial spawning, and continues to increase during and after the spawning season (1561).  Energy storage was highest between October and December, before the overwintering period (1561 1576), and lowest in July, during the spawning season in the Chesapeake Bay (1576).  Overwintering loss of energy is 33-35% of total body calories, derived primarily from deposits far in somatic and visceral tissues (1561).  This deposited visceral energy is considered critical to the success of surviving the winter and probably spawning (1576).  Wang (1576) also found an energy storage peak in August.  Spawning energy is derived primarily from feeding rather than energy reserves (1561).  The somatic weight component increases by 32-33% and total body weight by 26% during the spawning season, indicating that feeding provided enough energy to reproduce, and surplus for growth (1561 1576).

Maturation:  Bay anchovies become sexually mature during their first summer (794) attaining maturity at approximately 2.5 mo (311 1338) at 34-45 mm TL (255 197 754 1007).  Fives et al. (1554) support this theory by suggesting that bay anchovy, spawned early in the season, could grow to maturity and reach a size >40 mm SL, enabling them to spawn, during the first summer.  Luo and Musick (1551) observed that some bay anchovies have spawned as young as 2.5-3 months.

Zastrow et al. (1526), however, found that bay anchovy in the Chesapeake Bay were sexually mature at 40-45 mm FL, 10 months after hatching, and Age I fish, 35-42 mm FL, were immature and would not have spawned until the following year.  This may be a result of decreased developmental rates in colder temperatures.

Fecundity:  Size-specific fecundity is related to prey availability for adults, represented by a combination of abundance and patchiness in Tampa Bay (1566).  Fecundity of anchovies from the Delaware River Estuary was estimated at 13,250 eggs/female (1338).  Preliminary data using fish from the Chesapeake Bay population indicate that during the peak spawning period, virtually all females daily spawn a batch of eggs that can range from 514-2026, with the actual number directly related to the weight of the female (1526), approximately 400 eggs per gram of weight (1544).  This can result in a female producing 30,000 to 50,000 eggs during the four month season (1333).  Luo (1578) found that a female bay anchovy of average size was capable of producing 45,110 eggs, equivalent to 346% of body biomass energy.

Development (by life stage):
Egg:  Bay anchovy eggs are slightly elongated, with the major axis measuring 0.65-0.75 mm in length and is 0.1-0.8 mm longer than the minor axis (392).  The major and minor axes lengths decrease as salinity increases (794 1007 1571 1007).  Eggs are transparent, with no oil globule and the yolk composed of separate masses appearing as large cells (392 309 1548).  Yolk volume is 0.15 mm (342).  Eggs typically float at or near water surface until near hatching and then gradually sink (309 392 366).  Cleavage advances with great regularity and at a rapid rate (392).  Blastopore closes approximately 10 h after spawning with embryo slightly longer than 1/2 the greater circumference of the egg (392).  Soon after blastopore closure, Kupffer`s vesicle forms and embryo increases in length until it extends more than 2/3`s around the greater circumference of the yolk (392).  Incubation is approximately 24 h at 27.8 C (392 1530 1007).
Larva:  Larvae are 1.8-2.7 mm TL at hatching and weigh 17.6-6.0 g (174 342 392 754).  The yolk sac is comparatively large and greatly elongated, tapering to a point posteriorly (342 392 754).  Appearance shows a flattened, slender body, almost perfectly transparent with no evidence of pigmentation (342 392 754).  Larva is 2.6 to 2.8 mm TL after hatching (392).  Yolk mass retains elongated form and segmented character decreasing in size until it is absorbed 15 to 25 h after hatching, with post yolk sac larvae ranging from 2.7-16 mm (392 342 754).  Development of mouth and gut, pigmentation of eyes, and yolk exhaustion are completed simultaneously at 36 h after hatching at 26.2 C and 30.9 ppt (174 392 309).  No significant positive growth occurs until after yolk sac is depleted (1548).  Size at initial feeding is 2.9 mm SL (342).  A growth rate of 0.70 mm/d is reported after the fourth day from hatch (174).
	In laboratory experiments, larvae required high and stable food densities for survival.  Mean weight increased by 13.4 times from 17.6 micrograms at hatching to 236.0 micrograms at 16 days old with food densities maintained at 100 food organisms/larva (1334 1353).  Growth rates decrease as egg density increases (1558).  In a mesocosm enclosure experiment, Cowan and Houde (1558) found the rate of development was highest in an environment where initial egg density was the lowest.  Transformation into juvenile form begins at about 15.5 mm SL (366).
Young-of-Year:  Not applicable
Juvenile:  Limits of stage unknown, although metamorphosis is essentially complete by 22.5 mm SL (366 754).  A length of 18 mm TL is attained during the first month after hatch and growth of 10 mm/mo over the following 2 months is observed (197 116).

nodes.title: Length Range
nodes.body:
Egg: Eggs have a barely elliptical shape and are 0.84 to 1.11 mm in diameter (1532).
Larva: Larvae are 1.8-2.7 mm TL at hatching (174 342 392 754).  Size when feeding begins is 2.9 mm SL (1522).  Dorsal and anal fins start developing when larvae reach 5 mm TL, as some larvae have full ray counts a 7-8 mm SL (392). Also at 78 mm SL, larvae are transparent but have some pigmentation at the base of the anal fin and in the thoracic region (392).  In Florida, larval stage is completed at 15 mm SL (1580).
Young-of-Year:  Not applicable.
 Juvenile: Transformation into juvenile form begins at approximately 15 mm SL (366) and is essentially complete by 22.5 mm SL (1522).  The length range of juveniles in Florida is considered to be 15-30 mm SL by the Florida Fisheries Independent Monitoring Program (1580).  In Chesapeake Bay, the length range of juveniles considered to be 25-40 mm long (1568).
	A terminal mouth, short rounded maxillary not reaching the margin of the opercle, and absence of a definite silvery band differentiates juveniles from adults (312).  The characteristic projecting snout is developed at 20-25 mm (311).
Adult:  Bay anchovies measuring >30 mm SL are considered adults in Florida (1580).  Other reported sizes for adults range from 34-93 mm TL (224 193 255 550 588 664 751 561 709) with a mean of 56.3 mm TL for males and 60.0 mm TL for females (754).  The largest recored size was 100 mm (788).  Two, possibly three, size classes have been observed in wild fish populations but are virtually indistinguishable due to year round spawning (140 255 325 550).  Length distribution is variable on a monthly basis suggesting that maturation occurs early and the life span is short (226).

Length Conversions: A regression equation describing the standard length/total length relationship was presented by Matlock et al (1355):
[eq]
 	TL = 0.22391 + 1.20634 SL; 		(r^2 = 0.994)
[/eq]
Weight-Length Relationship:  The following length/weight equation was presented by Dawson (1354) based on measurements of 216 individuals:
[eq]
 	Log W = -4.76779 + 2.81451(Log L)
[/eq]
where W = weight in grams and L = length in mm.

Wet-Dry Weight Conversions:  Relationship between wet/dry weight (1541):
[eq]
 		ED = 691+156.3 DW
[/eq]
where ED = Energy Density (J/g wet weight) and DW = dry weight.

Length at Age: (by sex and sexes combined):
Larva:  Standard length of wild estuarine larvae increases exponentially at ~4% per day (d^(-1)) for the first 1.6 months, increasing from 0.24 mm d^(-1) on day 12 to 1.11 mm d^(-1) on day 49 (1554).
Juvenile:  Information not available.
Young-of-Year:  Even though most of the bay anchovy`s growth in length is complete by age 1+, significant increase in length and weight occur in older fish (1550).  Age I bay anchovy growth rates in Chesapeake Bay were 0.47 mm^(d-1) during Aug.-Oct. (1526).
Adult:  Bay anchovies attain maturity at approximately 2.5 months (311 1338) at 34-45 mm TL (197 255 754).

Longevity:  Annual mortality is high and few fish survive past age 2 (1550), sometimes to age 3 (1568).

nodes.title: Aging Structures/Methods
nodes.body: Growth Equations:  For the von Bertalanffy growth model, L and W are 165.28 mm and 33.57 g for females, and 156.06 mm and 27.93 g for males (1576).

nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body:
Commercial:  Bay anchovy are not currently harvested in United States due to their small size, but often used as bait or prepared as anchovy paste (116 159 309 311 312 794).  They apparently are not adversely affected by the commercial fisheries for other species, due to small size and ability to escape commercial nets (285 794 1337 1345).

Recreational:  This species is indirectly important to the sport fishing industry by serving as a major forage item (bait) for many food fish (309 116).

Ecological Role:  Bay anchovies probably constitute the greatest biomass of any fish in the estuarine waters of both the south Atlantic and the Gulf of Mexico (116 550 551 582 694 702 794 1061 1343).  This large population provides a major staple in the diet of many birds and fish (116 309 581 582 794 1337), as it accounts for more than half the energy intake of predatory fish in Chesapeake Bay from the spring through the fall (1568).  This species is the primary prey of the top 3 piscivores in Chesapeake Bay and of all planktivorous fishes there, is capable of consuming as much as 70-90% of the total zooplankton (1557).  The bay anchovy is a crucial link in the estuarine food web between zooplankton and higher trophic level predators (116 309 582 794 1524).  Due to its enormous trophic importance, this species is of particular interest to ecologists in terms of understanding estuarine food webs, community structure, and water quality restoration (1337 1568).

Distributions of predators indicate that the bay anchovy is an important prey species in the weedy shallows as well as bottom and surface waters (165).  In channel habitats in South Carolina, positive relationships were found between the bay anchovy and the Atlantic brief squid Lollifuncula brevis (1570).  This relationship is explained by one species enhancing the habitat for the other, the same response to similar environmental conditions, and cooperative social interactions (mixed schooling or the attraction of predators to prey) (1570).

Three schooling water-column species (gulf menhaden, bay anchovy, and tidewater silverside) inhabit the same estuarine environment, but occur independently due to environmental gradients, such as temperature, DO, and salinity (1540).  Since bay anchovy and other planktivorous fishes emigrate seaward and a significant portion do not return to estuaries the following spring, net biomass transfer is strongly in favor of export to the coastal ocean (1539).

Species Stress:  This species can quickly adapt to pollution stress due to its small size and short food chain and become the dominant species of the polluted area (39).  The bay anchovy is often the dominant species in areas of environmental stress (39 226 1344).

Ectoparasitic copepods, 15-40% of bay anchovy body length, present a hydrodynamic drag, causing considerable stress on the fishes (1537).

nodes.title: POPULATION
nodes.body:
Total Mortality:  The reported egg mortality rate of other anchovy species is less numerous and variable than that of the bay anchovy (1577).  Cohort mortality rates are lower in the middle of the spawning season (as food availability is maximum) and higher at end of spawning season, as food is less available (1556).

In the Chesapeake Bay, an average of 73% of spawned eggs died before hatching and of the surviving 27%, ~72% died during the 24h yolk-sac larval stage, indicating that >93% of cohorts die within 2 days (1564).  Overall mortality is greatest for eggs and very small larvae, as they are unable to avoid predation (1530 1576), and the overwinter period for Age I bay anchovy (1576).  Egg mortality rates are generally higher and more variable than larval rates (1335).  Major sources of early life stage mortality are predation and starvation (1335).  Newberger and Houde (1550) found that annual mortality rates in Chesapeake Bay for fully recruited juveniles and adults range from 89-95%.

Natural Mortality:  Piscivores and birds are the major cause of mortality, as medusae and ctenophores accounted for a significant portion of larval and egg mortality (1527 1568 456 1131).  Larval mortality rates in vegetated areas is largely associated with predation (1556).

Fishing Mortality:  Bay anchovy are not currently used in North America as human food and are not of direct commercial importance (794).  Bay anchovy are typically small enough to escape commercial fishing nets (794).

nodes.title: Annual Cohort Success
nodes.body:
Abundance by Month:  The highest abundance of bay anchovies is late summer and fall in Tampa Bay (664).  In a Mexican coastal  lagoon system, seasonal fluctuations in abundance were linked to preceding rain fluctuations and bay anchovy abundance peaked during the rainy season (1528).  Seasonal differences in larval bay anchovy abundance is highly correlated with densities of copepod nauplii (1546), although photoperiod, temperature, and salinity are considered to be influential factors as well (185).

Abundance by Year:  In the Indian River Lagoon, FL, bay anchovy were consistently collected throughout the year, with seasonal variations in abundance with influx of juveniles (1547).  The bay anchovy is virtually an annual species in Chesapeake Bay, so annual abundance is highly dependent on environmental factors and success of recruitment, as a single failed year-class could dramatically reduce population (1550).  Wang (1576) found in Chesapeake Bay that over 80% of all bay anchovy in all seasons were one year or less.  Maximum biomass is attained in the late postlarval or juvenile stages, due to high reproductive effort and high mortality rates (1550).

Vouglitois et al. (1560) supports the theory that population is largely regulated by the survival rate and migratory patterns of the overwintering populations rather than events occurring within estuaries during the first few months of life.  Opposition to this view, claiming that zooplankton fluctuations and ability for larvae to efficiently find prey, will more strongly influence population recruitment (1548 1559).  To support both these theories, Wang and Houde (1561) suggest that variability in future spawning biomass is dependent upon two periods of its annual cycle -- a) period of spawning recruitment, when predation is high, and b) winter.

Abundance by Area:

Population Abundance:  	Populations fluctuate from place to place and year to year, leaving no apparant trend in long-term abundance (1568).  Factors leading to total abundance and distribution are reproduction, habitat structure, diel period, season, and vegetation (1534).

Abundance and biomass peaks occur during late summer/early fall, resulting from rapid growth and recruitment of larvae and juveniles (1543).  Population density appears to be primarily influenced by prey density in Tampa Bay (1504) as well as other regions (582).  This probably accounts for their preference for bay habitats and when found in the Gulf, bay water masses (322).  Abundance patterns in the Great South Bay, New York shows that bay anchovies are the most abundant ichthyoplankter, totaling >96% of the eggs and >69% of the larvae collected (1546).  Olney (1535) found that the bay anchovy comprised 96% of total eggs and 88% of the larvae in his study in the lower Chesapeake Bay.  Although located within preferred habitats, abundance is not significantly correlated with salinity, temperature, DO, or turbidity (1528).  Castillo-Rivera et al. (1528) found in their study in a coastal lagoon in Mexico that there is a significant positive relationship between rainfall, and its associated influence on food availability with the lagoonal basin, and increase in bay anchovy abundance.

Management Regulations (by state and federal):  At the present time, there appears to be  little genetic evidence indicating a need for special protection or management intervention for bay anchovies (1531), as no commercial fishing pressure is currently influencing mortality and abundance (794).

nodes.title: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
nodes.body:
Competition:  Other estuarine plankton consumers, such as gulf menhaden (Brevoortia patronus), Atlanitc silversides (Menidia menidia), rough silversides (Membras martinica), striped anchovies (Anchoa hepsetus), blueback herring (Alosa aestivalis), ctenophores, and other jellyfish serve as potential competitors (1539 1540 1568).  But seasonal changes in species abundance and distribution, due to temperature, salinity, DO, and dietary preference, result in relatively little spatial overlap for comeptition (1539 1568).
Predation:  This large population provides a major staple in the diet of many birds and fish (116 309 581 582 794 1337 1568).  Distributions of predators indicate that the bay anchovy is an important prey species in the weedy shallows as well as surface and bottom waters (165).  Piscine predators include: Sciaenops ocellatus (red drum), Cynoscion arenarius (sand seatrout), C. nebulosus (spotted seatrout), C. regalia (weakfish), Bairdiella chrysura (silver perch), Centopomus undecimalis (snook); Strongylura marina (Atlantic needlefish), Synodus foetens (inshore lizardfish), Elops saurus (ladyfish), Ictalurus furcatus, Micropogonias undulatus (Atlantic croaker), Morone saxatilis (sptriped seabass), Paralichthys lethostigma (southern flounder), Pomatomus saltatrix (bluefish), and Caranx hippos (crevalle jack) (98 163 165 235 255 582 592 644 1337 1347 456 1131 1582).

In Chesapeake Bay, seasonal and localized abundance of bay anchovy eggs and ctenophores are reached together (1545), and yolk-sac larvae mortality rate is positively correlated with schysomedusae Chyrsaora quinquecirrha abundance (1577).  Medusae and ctenophores account for significant larval mortality (1527) and eggs, with medusae responsible for 26-100% of the predation in one study (1527).

Parasites/Diseases:  In Louisiana, postlarval bay anchovies were found to have ectoparasitic copepods attached on the dorsal surface between the pectoral and dorsal fins during warmer months in 10 ppt saline waters (1537).  Parasitic brachyurans (crabs) have been found attached to both larvae and juveniles (1529, as referenced in 1568).  Parasitic trematodes have been observed in adults located in the Chesapeake Bay (1568).

nodes.title: HUMAN IMPACTS
nodes.body:
Oil Spills:  Information not available

Contaminants:  There is little information on specific toxicants that adversely affect bay anchovy populations (1568).  However, the bay anchovy can quickly adapt and become the dominant species to pollution stressed areas, due to a short food chain and small size (1544 1568).  Dominance in a particular area for two or more consecutive seasons can indicated poor water quality (39).

Entrainment/Impingement: In Texas, Chung and Strawn (121) concluded that bay anchovy entrained and entrapped in an intake canal in a generating station, exposing them to heated effluent, could not survive in the cooling water system. The critically lethal period of the year was during the summer, as temperatures approached or exceeded 36C (121).  Water drawn for cooling at 74 m3 by way of a 3.7 km canal through three intake screens with 9.5 mm square openings, showed that 80% of impinged fish on screens were less than 50 mm in length (1538).  Most mortality related to intake and discharge of power plants occurs within the first six hours (1529, as cited in 1568).

Eutrophication:  Rain events, and subsequent eutrophication, have been correlated with peak abundances of bay anchovy in Pueblo-Viejo Lagoon, Veracruz, Mexico (1528).  Tampa Bay has a history of eutrophication, due to an overabundance of dissolved nutrients (1574), resulting in the bay anchovy to be the most abundant species found (1580).  In the Indian River Lagoon, the largest collections of mullet, Atlantic silversides, menhaden, Atlantic croaker, and bay anchovy occurred near periodic discharges of fresh water and nutrient materials from the St. Lucie Canal (848).

Pollutant Toxicity:  The bay anchovy is often the dominant species even in areas of environmental stress (39 226 1344).  Studies supported by the Texas Water Quality Board suggested that the bay anchovy may be useful to indicate poor water quality.  This species can quickly adapt to pollution stress due to its small size and short food chain and become the dominant species of the polluted area (39). Still, no information exists on specific pollutants or toxins that specifically impact bay anchovy population (1568).
